title: Influence
author: Robert Cialdini

parts.title: Click, whirr
text: Robert Cialdini begins with a confession: all his life he had been a patsy, the sort of person who ends up buying magazines he does not want and tickets to events he will not attend. As a psychologist at Arizona State University he studied why people say yes in the laboratory, and then, for nearly three years, he went undercover among the people who get yes for a living. He answered newspaper ads for sales trainees, learned to sell encyclopedias, vacuum cleaners, portrait photographs and dance lessons, and studied advertising and fund-raising from the inside.

What he found was a handful of principles that work because they usually serve us well. His first example is a friend who owned a jewellery shop in Arizona and could not sell a case of turquoise. Leaving town, she scribbled a note telling her head saleswoman to mark everything in the case at half price. The saleswoman misread it and doubled the prices, and the turquoise sold out. Tourists who knew little about turquoise were using a simple rule: expensive means good.

Animals run on such rules all the time. A mother turkey cares for her chicks when they make a cheep-cheep sound and ignores them when they do not. In one experiment she even mothered a stuffed polecat, her natural enemy, as long as it played a recording of that sound. Cialdini calls these automatic responses click, whirr: a trigger is pressed and a whole sequence of behaviour plays out.

People have their own. In a study by Ellen Langer, a woman asked to cut into a queue for a copying machine. When she said she had five pages and asked to go first because she was in a rush, 94 per cent let her. With no reason, 60 per cent did. When her reason was empty, because she had to make some copies, 93 per cent still agreed. The word because did most of the work. These shortcuts save us endless effort, and anyone who knows the trigger can press it.

parts.title: The debt we feel
text: The first principle is reciprocation: we feel obliged to repay what another person has given us. Cialdini calls it one of the most widespread rules of human culture. In 1985 Ethiopia, in the middle of a famine, sent 5,000 dollars of aid to Mexico after an earthquake there. The reason was that Mexico had helped Ethiopia when Italy invaded it in 1935, fifty years earlier.

Because the obligation is so strong, a small unwanted gift can produce a much larger return. Members of the Hare Krishna movement raised large sums in airports by pressing a flower into a traveller's hand, refusing to take it back, and then asking for a donation. Many travellers threw the flower in the nearest bin after paying; the Krishnas collected them and handed them out again. In an experiment by Dennis Regan, people who had been given a free soft drink by a stranger later bought twice as many raffle tickets from him as people given nothing, and they did so whether or not they liked him.

The rule also works through concessions. A request refused, followed by a smaller one, feels like a favour that deserves a favour in return. Cialdini was once stopped by a boy selling five-dollar tickets to a circus. When he declined, the boy asked whether he would buy some one-dollar chocolate bars instead. Cialdini bought two, though he does not like chocolate. In his own experiment, students asked to take a group of young offenders to the zoo for a day agreed 17 per cent of the time. When they were first asked to volunteer two hours a week for two years, and refused, 50 per cent agreed to the zoo trip.
The defence Cialdini suggests is to accept gifts and concessions politely, but to redefine them for what they are once they turn out to be sales tactics. A trick does not create a debt.

parts.title: Staying true to what we said
text: The second principle is commitment and consistency. Once we have taken a stand, we feel pressure to act in line with it, and we come to believe it more. People at a racetrack, for example, were more confident of their horse's chances just after placing a bet than just before.

In one experiment on a New York beach, a researcher spread a blanket near a stranger, listened to a radio for a while, and walked off. Another researcher then grabbed the radio and ran. Only 4 people out of 20 tried to stop him. But when the owner had first asked the neighbour to watch his things, 19 out of 20 gave chase, some of them physically. A small commitment had turned bystanders into guards.

Small commitments can lead to large ones. Researchers asked homeowners in California to put a huge, ugly sign reading DRIVE CAREFULLY in their front gardens, and 17 per cent agreed. Among homeowners who had agreed two weeks earlier to show a tiny sign about safe driving, 76 per cent agreed. The first yes had changed how they saw themselves: as people who care about such things. The Chinese used the same method on American prisoners during the Korean War, starting with requests for mild statements, such as that the United States is not perfect, then asking prisoners to read and expand them. Written commitments worked best, because they could be shown to others.

The pressure is strong enough to support many sales tricks. Toy companies advertise a few toys heavily before Christmas and ship too few of them. Parents who promised one buy other toys instead, and then, when the advertising returns in January, buy the promised toy as well. Car dealers offer a low price, let the buyer commit, then remove the advantage, and most buyers go through with the purchase. Cialdini's defence is to listen to the sinking feeling in the stomach that says a commitment is being used against you, and to ask whether, knowing what you know now, you would make the same choice again.

parts.title: Doing what others do
text: The third principle is social proof: when unsure what to do, we look at what people around us are doing. Television producers add canned laughter because audiences laugh more at jokes followed by it, even when they know it is fake and the jokes are weak. Bartenders put a few notes in the tip jar at the start of the evening, so that tipping looks like the done thing.

Social proof works most strongly under uncertainty, and that can be deadly. Cialdini describes the experiments of Bibb Latané and John Darley on bystanders. In one, a student who seemed to be having a seizure got help 85 per cent of the time when one other person heard it, and 31 per cent of the time when five others were present. Each person looked to the others for a cue, saw everyone else doing nothing, and concluded that nothing needed doing.

His advice for an emergency follows directly: do not appeal to a crowd. Pick one person, look at them, point, and give an instruction: you, in the blue jacket, call an ambulance. Once one person acts, others tend to follow.

The pull is strongest when the others are like us. The sociologist David Phillips found that after a suicide was reported on the front page, suicides rose in the area where the story ran, and so did car crashes and plane crashes, some of them disguised suicides. The rise was greatest among people similar to the person in the story. Cialdini's defence is to notice when the evidence of the crowd has been faked, as with laugh tracks and staged testimonials, and to look up from the crowd now and then to check the facts for ourselves.

parts.title: Saying yes to people we like
text: The fourth principle is liking. We prefer to say yes to people we know and like, and the people who make a living from yes know it. At a Tupperware party, the demonstrator sells, but the guests are buying partly from their friend the hostess, who gets a share of the sales. Joe Girard, whom the Guinness book named the world's greatest car salesman, sent every one of his past customers a greeting card each month that said simply that he liked them.

Several things make us like people, and each can be used. Physical attractiveness works like a halo: in Canadian federal elections in 1974, attractive candidates received more than two and a half times as many votes as unattractive ones, while voters denied that looks had influenced them. We like people who resemble us, even in small things such as clothing, which is why salespeople are trained to look for similarities. We like people who compliment us, even when we can tell the praise is not true.

Contact helps when it is pleasant, and cooperation helps most. In a famous experiment at a boys' summer camp, Muzafer Sherif turned two groups of boys into bitter rivals through competition. Contact alone did not reduce the hostility. What did was a series of problems that the groups could solve only by working together.

We are also influenced by association. People blame weather forecasters for bad weather, as though the messenger had caused the message. Sports fans say we won after a victory and they lost after a defeat; Cialdini found that university students wore their school's clothing more often after the team had won. His defence against the whole principle is simple: when you find you like someone more than you would expect after a short acquaintance, separate the person from the deal, and judge the deal on its merits.

parts.title: Obeying the uniform
text: The fifth principle is authority. We are trained from childhood to defer to legitimate experts, and usually this makes sense. But the deference can become automatic. In Stanley Milgram's experiments, about two thirds of ordinary volunteers kept giving what they believed were painful electric shocks to a protesting man, up to the highest level, because a researcher in a grey lab coat told them to continue.

Doctors carry this kind of authority. In one study, a researcher telephoned hospital nurses, introduced himself as a doctor they did not know, and ordered them to give a patient twice the maximum dose of a drug that was not on the approved list. In 95 per cent of cases the nurse went to give it before being stopped. Cialdini also tells of a doctor who ordered ear drops for a patient's right ear, abbreviated on the prescription as R ear. The nurse put the drops in the patient's rectum, and neither she nor the patient questioned it.

Often the symbols of authority are enough without the substance. Robert Young, an actor who played a doctor on television, sold large amounts of coffee in advertisements by advising people, as a doctor might, to drink a decaffeinated brand. Titles and clothes are enough to trigger deference. In one study, people were three and a half times more likely to follow a man crossing the street against the light when he wore a suit and tie than when he wore work clothes.

The defence Cialdini proposes is two questions. Is this authority really an expert on the matter in hand, or only dressed like one? And how truthful can we expect this expert to be here, given what they gain? A salesperson who admits a small drawback in a product before praising it is often using honesty as a tactic.

parts.title: Wanting what we might lose
text: The sixth principle is scarcity. Opportunities seem more valuable when they are less available, and the thought of losing something moves us more than the thought of gaining something of the same value. Salespeople use it constantly: only a few left, or the offer ends on Friday.

Part of the effect is a shortcut, since things that are hard to get usually are better. Part of it is what psychologists call reactance: when our freedom to have something is limited, we want it more. It appears in two-year-olds and in teenagers forbidden to see someone, and Cialdini notes research suggesting that parents who oppose a young couple's romance can deepen it. When Miami banned detergents containing phosphates, residents drove to other counties to stock up and judged the banned detergents to work better than before.

Scarcity works best when something becomes newly scarce, and when we must compete for it. In an experiment, people rated cookies from a jar of two as more desirable than identical cookies from a jar of ten, and rated them higher still when the jar had just gone from ten to two. A beef importer told some of his customers that a shortage of Australian beef was coming; they ordered twice as much as usual. Those also told that the news came from an exclusive source ordered six times as much.

Cialdini closes the book by defending the shortcuts themselves. Life moves too fast for anyone to think through every decision, and these rules are mostly reliable. The danger is people who fake the signals: the invented deadline, the paid testimonial, the actor in a white coat. His advice is to stay alert to the rush of feeling that a shortcut produces, and to remember that the thing we want is worth what it is worth, scarce or not. The cookies from the nearly empty jar, he reminds us, did not taste any better.
